overview: This file documents the intensifying 1939 controversy over American economic support for Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. It brings together petitions, constituent letters, religious and civic campaigns, congressional inquiries, Chinese criticism, press coverage, opinion polling, diplomatic reporting, trade statistics, corporate correspondence, and extensive State Department legal and policy analysis. Throughout much of the file, officials emphasize that existing neutrality legislation and the Nine-Power Treaty did not empower the president to impose a general embargo on petroleum, scrap metal, and other strategic goods without congressional action. By December, however, the record shifts from explanations of legal restraint to an informal exercise of executive influence: the Department coordinated a voluntary “moral embargo” under which American petroleum and engineering firms were asked to withhold high-octane aviation-fuel processes, equipment, technical assistance, and certain blending agents from Japan and the Soviet Union. Subsequent papers trace corporate compliance, continuing export monitoring, contractual complications, and Japan’s diplomatic protest.
keywords: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
interest: The file is especially valuable for showing how foreign policy emerged from pressure exerted by citizens, churches, missionaries, advocacy organizations, legislators, journalists, diplomats, lawyers, and private corporations—not simply from decisions at the top of the administration. Its legal memoranda reveal the gap between widespread demands to “stop arming Japan” and the executive branch’s limited statutory authority, while the aviation-gasoline papers show officials developing a voluntary, company-by-company alternative to formal sanctions. Detailed corporate disclosures, technical assessments, trade data, accounts of Japanese bombing, and Japan’s eventual protest make the collection unusually useful for tracing both the moral politics and the practical machinery of economic pressure before the broader U.S. embargoes of the early 1940s.
